title: Not money, fame, pleasure or power (ST I-II.2)
hookLine: Thomas tests each and none can satisfy

cards: There's a voice that says it: just one more. One more raise, and then the money will feel like enough. One more round of applause, and you'll feel like you matter.
One more weekend away, one more title on the door, one more good meal, and then, finally, you'll rest. Then the raise comes, and the bar quietly moves. So where is happiness?
Thomas runs something like a lab test. He lines up the usual candidates and checks each one. Today: not money.

teach.h: MONEY IS ALWAYS FOR SOMETHING ELSE.
teach.b: Money goes first. It's always for something else: food, a roof, the things it buys. Anything wanted only as a means can't be the end you're looking for.

Next, honor and fame. Honor is given because of a good someone already has, so it's a sign of the good, not the good itself. And fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong, and gone by morning.
Then power. It can be used well or terribly, and anything that can be used for evil can't be the highest good, which no one could misuse. Then pleasure.

teach.h: POWER CAN BE MISUSED; PLEASURE FOLLOWS.
teach.b: Pleasure is real, and good, but it follows something good, the way a glow follows a fire. Chase the glow by itself and you lose the fire. Then the big turn.
Why does every candidate fail? Not because these things are bad; Thomas calls them goods. They fail because they're limited, and the will is made for the good without limit.
Every created good is a part.

teach.h: EACH GOOD IS A PART; THE WILL WANTS THE WHOLE.
teach.b: The will wants the whole. So the hunger outruns everything we feed it. Jesus puts it sharply, in the Douay-Rheims: "For what doth it profit a man, if he gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his own soul?"

teach.h: WHERE THY TREASURE IS, THERE IS THY HEART.
teach.b: And he names the mechanism: "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also." Thomas's conclusion: only God can fill it. Tomorrow, what that would look like.
Today, just the sorting: good things, real things. Not the thing.

how: Catholic teaching, following Thomas, holds that riches, honor, power and pleasure are real goods but cannot by themselves make a person happy, and this sorting appears in retreats, homilies and teaching on the beatitudes.

o: no limited good can be the whole of happiness
having money is always a sin in itself
wealth and fame are wrong to enjoy at all

p: a sign of a good, not the good
follows a good, like a glow

s: Thomas says money, fame, power and pleasure are evil
he calls them real goods. they fail as happiness because they're limited, and the will wants the good without limit.
for Thomas, pleasure follows something good rather than being the goal itself
like a glow following a fire. chase the glow alone and you lose the fire.
Thomas rules out power because nobody can use it well
power can be used well or badly. because it can be misused, it can't be the highest good.

games.q: you're Thomas, testing fame as the answer to happiness. what's the problem with it?
o: fame lives in other people's heads, where it can be wrong and can vanish.
fame is the answer; the test passes.
games.why: Thomas says fame depends on what others know of you, which can be mistaken and passing. it can't be the lasting good the will wants.

practice: Look back over the last few days and name one place your attention kept running: the account balance, the likes, the next treat.
Ask Thomas's questions of it: is this for something else, and if I got all of it, would I stop wanting?
Don't throw it away; set it down at its proper size, a good thing, not the whole thing, and if you pray, hand that chase to God for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Not money. Thomas tests money, fame, power and pleasure, and finds each a real good that can't be the whole of happiness. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: happiness, blessedness — what Thomas is testing each candidate against.

carryVoice: Your line: none of these. Good things, every one, just not the whole. That's today, done.
